items.headline: Restricted Nvidia Blackwell chips found running in a Shanghai data centre
items.what: Chinese regulatory filings show that two firms installed Nvidia Blackwell hardware, a GB300 NVL72 rack and a GB200 server, at a Shanghai data centre known as the Yangtze River Delta Project. The filings, reviewed by Bloomberg, list the hardware as collateral for bank loans. Shipping Blackwell chips to China needs a United States export licence, and the site is linked to Alice Huang, founder of the Singapore cloud firm Megaspeed, which Washington placed on a trade blacklist this month over chip diversion concerns. Bloomberg found no evidence that Megaspeed itself moved the hardware to the site, and how the chips reached China is not known.
items.why: The filings are the first documented evidence that Nvidia's most powerful data centre chips are operating inside China despite the export ban, and they land days after Nvidia told partners to pause AI server shipments to four Southeast Asian countries while it checks the same rules. The case shows how hard the controls are to enforce when hardware moves through intermediaries.

items.headline: Boston Scientific breach exposes personal and medical details of about 118,000 people
items.what: Medical device maker Boston Scientific is notifying people affected by a cyberattack on its cloud systems. The attacker used a voice phishing call to reach the company's cloud infrastructure, and the intrusion exposed personal details, Social Security numbers, government ID numbers, medical information and health insurance details of 117,789 people. The intrusion took place in May, and the company confirmed in November that personal data had been exposed. Patient medical records and data from remote monitoring and connected devices were not exposed. The company says the incident did not disrupt manufacturing, ordering or patient services, and it is the company's second cyber incident this year after an August attack that disrupted operations.
items.why: The breach combines identity details with medical and insurance information, which is the kind of record that is hard for victims to change and useful for fraud. It also shows how a single phone call aimed at an employee can open a path into a large company's cloud systems, which is why the attack method matters as much as the data taken.

items.headline: pCloud confirms cyberattack on its password manager after suspicious login warnings
items.what: Cloud storage provider pCloud has confirmed a cyberattack on pCloud Pass, its password manager. Customers reported warnings that an unfamiliar device had connected to their accounts, including some who had two factor authentication switched on. pCloud says the attack was contained quickly, that a small number of user email addresses were exposed and login attempts were made, and that its cloud storage service was not affected. The company says passwords and notes stored in the manager were not compromised because they are encrypted on customer devices, but it has not said whether any encrypted vaults were accessed or taken.
items.why: Password managers hold the keys to a person's online accounts, so an attack on one draws attention even when the stored passwords are not confirmed taken. The incident is the third password manager attack reported this month, after similar disclosures from mSecure and 1Password, and it is a reminder to watch for phishing messages that follow a breach.

items.headline: OpenAI countersues Apple over trade secrets in AI hardware fight
items.what: OpenAI has filed counterclaims against Apple in federal court in San Jose, California, accusing Apple of stealing its trade secrets and pressuring shared hardware suppliers. The filing says a former OpenAI employee who returned to Apple sent more than a hundred confidential files about an unreleased OpenAI device to personal accounts, and that Apple asked suppliers to identify staff working on OpenAI projects and pressed at least one vendor to stop work. OpenAI also says Apple uses employment and exit rules that make it hard for departing staff to separate work files from personal files. Apple denies the claims and says OpenAI is trying to distract from its own lawsuit, in which OpenAI was ordered to stop using Apple confidential information. The dispute began in July, when Apple sued OpenAI and two former Apple employees, saying they carried Apple hardware secrets to OpenAI.
items.why: The countersuit turns a one-sided lawsuit into a two-way fight between the two companies racing to build AI hardware, and it puts supplier relationships and hiring rules at the centre of that race. How the court rules will shape whether OpenAI can build its planned AI devices with the suppliers it needs, and whether Apple can keep its former staff and their knowledge from reaching a rival.
